After considering the submissions of the parties and perusal of the documents placed on record, the following issues arise for consideration: # **Issue No. 1: Whether the Commission has jurisdiction to entertain the present Petition?** We now proceed to discuss the above issues and examine the claims of the Petitioner. # **Issue No. 1: Whether the Commission has jurisdiction to entertain the present Petition?** 15. At the outset, the Respondents have submitted that the present Petition is not maintainable before this Commission on the ground of a lack of jurisdiction. They have placed the reliance on the judgement of APTEL in _Southern Power Distribution Company of AP Limited vs. Andhra Pradesh State Electricity Regulatory Commission and Anr., Appeal No. 397 of 2022_ and submitted that the in the light of the clause(s) in the Purchase Orders and the law laid down by the APTEL in the said Judgment, the appropriate forum for adjudicating the present dispute is the Telangana State Electricity Regulatory Commission (TSERC) only. multiple States and had a composite scheme of generation and supply of electricity in more than one State. Given that the dispute, as brought up in the present Petition pertains to the inter-state transactions, this Commission has the necessary jurisdiction to entertain the present Petition in light of the ratio laid down by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Energy Watchdog Judgment. # **Issue No. 2: Whether the Petitioner’s claim for LPS is barred by limitation?** 22. Whereas, the Petitioner has submitted that the contention of the Respondents as regards the claims/reliefs claimed being barred by limitation is erroneous and untenable. The supply of power between the parties ended only on 31.3.2020. This is a case of an executory contract where a running account is maintained, and the accounts have to be settled only upon termination of the agreement between the parties. The last date for payment for power purchase pertained to May 2020, and the Respondents made the corresponding payment, excluding the LPS, only on 25.3.2021. Hence, the claim of the Petitioner for LPS is not barred by limitation. The due date of the last invoice for LPS was 16.4.2021, and this petition was filed on 8.8.2023, which is well within the limitation period of 3 years. 23. We have considered the submissions of the Petitioner and the Respondents on the limitation and find that the said objection, as raised by the Respondents, is misconceived. Pertinently, the APTEL in the Udupi Judgment ( _Appeal No. 10 of 2020 and batch titled Power Company of Karnataka Ltd. v. Udupi Power Corporation Ltd.)_ as regards the claim for the LPS being a ‘continuing wrong’ has held that a “continuing wrong” includes a continuing source of injury and renders the doer of the act responsible and liable for the continuance of the said injury. Further, the APTEL has held that every time a breach is committed, the aggrieved party gets a fresh cause of action to invoke appropriate judicial proceedings and that the default of the distribution licensee to pay the LPS partakes the character of a continuing breach as contemplated with the said Purchase Orders. It is not disputed that there was a delay on the part of the Respondents in making the timely payment towards the said bills and that they have not paid the LPS claimed by the Petitioner for this period of delay. Further, the Respondents have not submitted any document/correspondence on record to show that either the bills or the LPS bills have been disputed by the Respondents. In the absence of any such dispute, the liability to pay the LPS stands admitted by the Respondents.
